t.1.41.1: At this very time, the sage Jaratkāru, of great austerities, wandered over the whole earth, making his home wherever evening found him.
t.1.41.2: Practising a vow hard to keep for those of undisciplined self, the one of great splendour wandered about, bathing at the holy tīrthas.
t.1.41.3: Living on air, without food, the sage was withering away day by day. He saw his ancestors hanging face downward in a pit.
t.1.41.5: Approaching those wretched ones, who were without food, emaciated, miserable and suffering in the pit, longing for rescue, he, himself wretched in appearance, addressed them.
t.1.41.4: He saw them clinging to a clump of vīraṇa grass of which only a single fibre remained, and a rat that dwelt in a hole slowly gnawing away at that very fibre.
t.1.41.6: Who are you, sirs, who hang clinging to this clump of vīraṇa grass, weakened because its roots have been gnawed away by a rat that dwells in a hole?
t.1.41.7: Even that single root which still remains here in the clump of vīraṇa grass, this rat is slowly gnawing away with its sharp teeth.
t.1.41.9: Then sorrow arose in me upon seeing you hanging head downward, fallen into grievous distress. What kindness may I do for you?
t.1.41.8: Since only a little of it remains, it will soon cut through this too, and then you are bound to fall here, head downward, into this pit.
t.1.41.10: Tell me without delay: is it with a fourth of this austerity of mine, or again with a third, or even with half, that you may cross over this calamity?
t.1.41.11: Or else, let all of you, sirs, cross over from this place by means of my entire austerity; let it be arranged thus, as you wish.
t.1.41.12: Prosperous indeed are you, a brahmacārin, who wish to save us here; but, O foremost of Brahmins, this cannot be removed by austerity.
t.1.41.13: We do have the fruit of our austerities, dear son, O best of speakers; but because our line of offspring is dying out, O brahmin, we are falling into an impure hell.
t.1.41.14: As we hang here, dear son, no knowledge dawns on us, and so we do not recognize you, whose manly valor is renowned in the world.
t.1.41.16: We are seers named the Yāyāvaras, of rigorous vows, O mighty one; we have fallen here from the holy world because of the failure of our lineage.
t.1.41.15: Blessed are you, illustrious one, who out of compassion have come near and grieve for us, pitiable and deeply afflicted as we are. Hear, O twice-born one, who we truly are.
t.1.41.17: Our holy merit of austerity is lost, for we have no thread of descent at all. True, we have one thread today, but he too is as good as not existing.
t.1.41.18: In our family, we of little fortune have, it is said, a kinsman, himself unfortunate, known as Jaratkāru, who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, self-controlled, great-souled, firm in his vows, and of exceedingly great austerity.
t.1.41.19: Through his greed for austerity, he has brought us into this distress; he has no wife, no son, nor any kinsman at all.
t.1.41.20: Therefore we hang in this pit, bereft of our senses, like men who have no protector. When you see him, you should speak to him, so that we may have a protector.
t.1.41.21: Your forefathers hang in the pit, wretched and head downward; tell him, O mighty one, 'Take a wife, as is right,' and 'Beget offspring,' for you alone, O ascetic rich in austerity, are the one thread of our lineage that remains.
t.1.41.22: O brahmin, the clump of vīraṇa grass that you see us clinging to was the stock of our family, the one who would increase his own lineage.
t.1.41.23: The roots of this plant that you see here, O brahmin, are the threads of our lineage, dear son, which have been devoured by Time.
t.1.41.24: This root of it that you see, O brahmin, half eaten away, is what we all hang from; and he too, the only one left, has given himself up to austerity.
t.1.41.25: The rat that you see, O brahmin, is mighty Time; gnawing slowly and little by little, he is wearing away that man devoted to austerities, Jaratkāru, who is greedy for austerity, dull-minded and senseless.
t.1.41.26: For that austerity of his will not save us, O best of the virtuous. See us, cut off at the root, fallen, our minds stricken by time, set firmly on the path to hell just like evil-doers.
t.1.41.28: Austerity, or sacrifice, or whatever else is greatly purifying, all of that is not equal to offspring, dear son; such is the opinion of the good.
t.1.41.27: When we have fallen here together with our ancestors of old, he too, cut down by Time, will surely go to hell here thereafter.
t.1.41.29: Dear one, when you see the ascetic Jaratkāru, you should speak to him; and all this, just as you have seen it, must be told to him by you in full.
t.1.41.30: O brahmin, you should speak to him in such a way that he takes wives and begets sons, so that we may have a protector.
